sentences: This is Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land by An Gyeon.
Across a long silk handscroll, rocky mountains roll on like waves.
Somewhere at the end of them lies a utopia that a prince once saw in a dream.
The calligraphy at the far left was written by Prince Anpyeong, third son of King Sejong.
He records a dream on the night of the twentieth day of the fourth month in 1447.
In it, he wandered with friends such as Bak Paeng-nyeon into a valley of peach blossoms.
When the prince described his dream, the court painter An Gyeon turned it into this scroll in just three days.
It is painted in ink and light colour on silk, 38.
7 centimetres high and 106.
5 centimetres long.
Most East Asian handscrolls are unrolled and read from right to left, but this one begins at the left.
The low, gentle earthen hills in the lower left stand for the ordinary world, the one we live in every day.
Move toward the centre and the mountains suddenly turn harsh.
Strange rocky peaks shoot upward and a narrow, steep gorge winds between them.
You can almost feel in your legs that the road to paradise is never easy.
The rock faces are built from layer upon layer of curling, cloud-like ink strokes, a manner traced to the Northern Song painter Guo Xi.
Your eye climbs on a diagonal, from the lower left toward the upper right.
At the far right, a broad valley ringed by peaks like a folding screen: this is the Peach Blossom Land.
Blossoms fill the mist and a few small houses stand quietly.
Yet not a single person or animal appears anywhere.
The everyday world is seen straight on, while the paradise is seen from high above.
Several viewpoints are stitched seamlessly into one picture, so looking at it feels like walking through a dream, where the ground keeps shifting beneath you.
After the painting come the prince's own texts and poems by some twenty of the finest scholars of the day, among them Sin Suk-ju, Bak Paeng-nyeon and Seong Sam-mun.
Counting one monk, there are twenty-three tributes in all.
That makes the scroll a time capsule of early Joseon culture at its height, with painting, poetry and calligraphy side by side.
Today it belongs to the Tenri University Central Library in Japan, and it has been shown in Korea only on rare occasions.
Now step back and walk slowly with your eyes, from the soft hills on the left to the hidden valley on the right.
In the paradise the prince found in his dream, where would you choose to stop and stay?
